1.pericope_label: Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; the elder women as mothers, the younger as sisters

schools.summary: Robertson settles the sense of the noun and the force of the verb together. The dative is used in the usual sense of an older man, not a minister or bishop, as is shown by the following words 'as a father'; and the verb is a first aorist ingressive active subjunctive with the negative, a prohibition against committing the act, of a verb meaning to strike upon — an old word occurring here only in the New Testament, and here in the figurative sense of striking with words rather than with fists. Respect for age, he says, is what is commanded. On the following clause he notes that the comparative adjective is anarthrous, 'younger men', and calls these wise words for the young minister, who must know how to conduct himself with old men in reverence and with young men in fellowship, without stooping to folly with them; and on the last clause he adds the warning that no sort of behaviour will so easily make or mar the young preacher as his conduct with young women. Ellicott marks the turn the Epistle takes here, from the public duties connected with the office of superintending presbyter to the private relations which one in Timothy's position ought to maintain with individual members of the congregation; and the first thing warned against is a misplaced zeal. The enthusiastic and ardent young servant of Christ would see with sorrow and dismay the shortcomings of many an elder member of his flock, and, forgetting to make wise allowance for previous training, thought and habits, would be likely, unwisely and possibly unfairly, to find fault; let him instead use respectful and affectionate entreaties, after the manner of a son and not of an official. Ellicott also confirms that the reference is rather to age than to office, since the reminder about the elder women follows. Barnes gives the most searching note on the closing phrase: nothing could be more characteristic of Paul's manner, and nothing show a deeper acquaintance with human nature, for the Apostle knew the danger which would beset a youthful minister when it was his duty to admonish a youthful female, and the scandal to which he might be exposed if in the performance of his office there should be the slightest departure from purity and propriety. He was therefore to guard his heart with more than common vigilance, and to indulge in no word, look or action which could by any possibility be construed as manifesting an improper state of feeling.

Gill takes the elder for one in years and not in office, since elders by office are spoken of later in the chapter with rules of their own, and since the word here stands opposed not to a private member of a church but to young men in age. On the verb he is vivid: the word signifies to smite or strike, and the Arabic version renders it 'do not strike an elder' — meaning not with the hand but with the tongue, since giving hard words is as heavy blows. Reproof is a smiting, and there is a gentle one and a sharp one, and it is with the former that a man in years is to be reproved when he is in a fault, whether with respect to doctrine or to practice. On the elder women Gill says they are to be reasoned and argued and pleaded with as children should with their mothers, being considered as mothers in Israel and treated with great tenderness and respect. Calvin explains the rule as a matter of dosage: correction is a medicine which has always some bitterness and is consequently disagreeable, and Timothy being a young man his severity would have been less tolerable had it not been somewhat moderated. It is impossible not to be moved with reverence when we place before our eyes our father or our mother, so that instead of harsher vehemence we are immediately influenced by modesty. Yet Calvin adds a caution: the Apostle does not wish old men to be spared or indulged in such a manner as to sin with impunity and without correction, but only that some respect should be paid to their age, that they may more patiently bear to be admonished. The vinegar must always be mingled with the oil, though with this difference, that reverence should always be shown to older persons and equals treated with brotherly gentleness — from which Calvin draws the lesson for pastors, that they must not only take into account their office but see particularly what is due to the age of individuals, for the same things are not applicable to all.

Henry treats the passage as a rule of proportion in reproving. Ministers are reprovers by office — it is a part, though the least pleasing part, of their office, since they are to preach the word and to reprove and rebuke — and a great difference is to be made in our reproofs according to the age, quality and other circumstances of the persons rebuked. The rule has four parts. Elders in age or office are to be treated very tenderly, respect being had to the dignity of their years and place, so that they must not be rebuked sharply nor magisterially; and Timothy himself, though an evangelist, must entreat them as fathers, this being the likeliest way to work upon them and to win upon them. The younger must be rebuked as brethren, with love and tenderness, not as one desirous to spy faults or pick quarrels but as one willing to make the best of them — for there is need of a great deal of meekness in reproving those who deserve reproof. The elder women must be reproved, when there is occasion, as mothers; and the younger women as sisters, with all purity.

Clarke takes the word in its natural sense of one advanced in years, noting that at the seventeenth verse it is taken in what may be termed its ecclesiastical meaning and signifies an officer in the Church, since the terms were sometimes confounded. There are but few cases, he says, in which it at all becomes a young man to reprove an old man, and especially one who is a father in the Church: if such a one does wrong or gets out of the way, he should be entreated as a father, with great caution and respect, to which at least his age entitles him; and the verb means do not smite, that is, do not treat them harshly nor with magisterial austerity. The younger men are to be treated as brethren, showing humility and arrogating nothing to oneself on account of one's office. Clarke then widens the whole passage into a plea for patience in discipline: feel for every member of the Church, old and young, male and female, consider them as fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters, treat them all with gentleness, and labour to keep them in, not to expel them from, the Church. There are some, he adds, who seem to take a barbarous pleasure in expelling members; but while they are in the Church, under its ordinances and discipline, there is some hope that their errors may be corrected, and once driven out into the world that hope must necessarily become extinct — so that, as judgment is God's strange work, excommunication should be the strange, the last, and the most reluctantly performed work of every Christian minister. Wesley states the ground of the whole in a clause: rebuke not, considering your own youth, with such a severity as would otherwise be proper.

3.pericope_label: Honour widows that are widows indeed; but if any widow have children or nephews, let them requite their parents

schools.summary: Robertson distinguishes the two groups the chapter treats: in the verses beginning here Paul discusses widows who are in distress, and in those that follow, widows who are in the employment of the local church for certain work; and evidently, as at the first forming of the church at Jerusalem, so here at Ephesus some trouble had arisen over the widows. The verb is a present imperative, keep on honouring, and Timothy is to show proper respect both for individual cases of need and for the class. Barnes explains why the office existed at all, and does it from the social conditions: the intercourse of the sexes was much more circumscribed in oriental countries than among us, access to the female members of the church would be much less free, and there might therefore have been a special propriety in entrusting the duty of watching over the younger among them to the more aged. That duty would naturally be committed to those who had not the care of families, and, if they were qualified, to those who had not the means of support, who while maintained by the church might be rendering a valuable service to it. On the fourth verse he settles the word rendered nephews: it now commonly means the son of a brother or sister, though formerly the English word also meant grandchildren, and the Greek denotes those sprung or born of, embracing only those in a direct line — so that it would not properly include nephews and nieces at all. Ellicott sets the whole matter in the history of women's work, arguing that Christianity had during the thirty years of its history developed a perfectly new existence for women who professed the faith: in the Master's new and strange command that the poor and needy and sick should be succoured, a blessed calling was invented for Christian women, whose secluded and in many respects degraded life in the old world was in great measure owing to the fact that till Christ taught the universal duty of charity they had no recognised public occupation. He agrees that the word should be rendered grandchildren, and reads the verse as a warning against allowing the Church to be burdened with what others ought to bear, a solemn and imperative duty not to be evaded by any bearing the Christian name.

Clarke settles what the honour is by the word itself: one meaning of the verb is to support or sustain, and here it is most obviously to be taken in this sense — provide for those widows especially which are widows indeed, persons truly destitute, being aged and helpless, having neither children nor friends to take care of them, and who behave as becometh their destitute state. On the following verse he draws the inference the other way: the mention of children or grandchildren shows that widows indeed are those who have neither, that is, no relatives who either will or can help them, or none near enough alive. Let these children and grandchildren provide for their aged or helpless relatives, and not burden the Church with them while they are able to support them. The command to requite their parents Clarke renders as a giving of benefit for benefit: your parents supported and nourished you when you were young and helpless, and you ought therefore to support them when they are old and destitute — this being what is called showing piety, in which he hears an allusion to the fifth commandment, which requires that father and mother be honoured and provided for in their old age and afflictions. Wesley reduces the first command to four words, that to honour is to maintain out of the public stock.

Gill first rules out an alternative reading of the honour: it is not a putting of them into the office of a deaconess in the church, an office some think is referred to later and which did obtain in some of the primitive churches — for it might be that some of these widows were preferred to the rest and set over them, having the care of such as were more infirm, but that could only be the case of some, whereas the honour here spoken of is to be given to all that are really widows. It therefore rather regards some external honour and respect to be shown them by words and actions, and especially an honourable provision for them and maintenance of them. Gill supports the usage from Jewish custom, where giving gifts to persons and making presents to them is itself called honour. On the following verse he states the rule plainly: widows who have children or grandchildren are not widows indeed, since they are not desolate or alone or without persons to take care of them, and their children should provide for them and not suffer the church to be burdened with them.

Henry reads the command as concerning admission to an office and a maintenance together: to honour widows that are widows indeed is to maintain them and to admit them into office, there having been in those times an office in the church in which widows were employed, namely to tend the sick and the aged and to look to them by the direction of the deacons. He points to the care taken of widows immediately upon the first forming of the Christian church, when the Grecians thought their widows were neglected in the daily ministration and the provision made for poor widows. The general rule, he says, is to honour widows that are widows indeed — to maintain them, and to relieve them with respect and tenderness; and he notes that only those widows were to be relieved by the charity of the church who were pious and devout, and not wanton widows that lived in pleasure. She is to be reckoned a widow indeed, and to be maintained at the church's charge, who, being desolate, trusteth in God.

5.pericope_label: She that is a widow indeed trusteth in God; but she that liveth in pleasure is dead while she liveth

schools.summary: Barnes guards the first description against being read too darkly: the word rendered desolate means solitary or alone, and does not necessarily imply the idea of discomfort which we attach to the English word, the sense being that she had no children or other descendants, none on whom she could depend for support. She has no one else to look to but God; having no earthly reliance, and destitute of husband, children and property, she feels her dependence and steadily looks to God for consolation and support; and the phrase 'night and day' means continually, as in the description of Anna in the Gospel. On the contrasting figure Barnes explains the Greek verb, which occurs only once elsewhere in the New Testament and properly means to live in luxury, voluptuously, to indulge freely in eating and drinking and to yield to the indulgence of the appetites — it does not indicate grossly criminal pleasures, but the kind of pleasure connected with luxurious living and with pampering the appetite. It is probable, he adds, that in the time of the apostle there were professedly Christian widows who lived in this manner, as there are such professing Christians of all kinds in every age of the world; and 'dead while she liveth' means that to all the proper purposes of life she is as if she were dead, nothing conveying more forcibly the truth that true happiness is not to be found in the pleasures of sense. Robertson supplies the grammar: the participle rendered desolate is a perfect passive, left alone, a verb found here alone in the New Testament, describing one without husband, children or other close kin; the verb of hoping is a perfect active, she has placed her hope on God and keeps it there; and the words 'night and day' are genitive, meaning by night and by day, so that Paul does not say she should pray all night and day. Ellicott returns from the exception to the class itself, a class no doubt often utterly neglected in those days of selfish luxury and extreme misery, and not unfrequently left to starve; and on the contrasting figure he calls the widow who could so forget her sorrow and her duty a living corpse, sharply contrasted with her far happier sister who, dead to the pleasures of the flesh and living a life of prayer and self-denial, may in the true sense of the word be spoken of as living. He notes that the greatest of the Greek poets used the same figure to the opposite end, counting the man who gives up pleasures a living corpse.

Clarke reads the first description as a chain of cause and effect: she is left entirely alone, having neither children nor relatives to take care of her, and finding she has no other helper she continues in prayer and supplication, that she may derive from God what in the course of his providence he has deprived her of among men. On the widow who lives in pleasure he agrees with the others that the fault is luxury rather than lewdness — she lives delicately, voluptuously indulging herself with dainties, the phrase not indicating grossly criminal pleasures but simply one who indulges herself in good eating and drinking, pampering her body at the expense of her mind. He then illustrates the word from an unexpected quarter, since it is used in reference to what we term petted and spoiled children, and quotes an ancient letter on the boy who, if he have not food when and as he pleases, bursts out into weeping; who if he eats must have dainties and sweetmeats; who complains of fatigue if the weather be hot and trembles if it be cold; who scolds if he be reproved, and is enraged if everything be not provided for him according to his wish. On the charge that follows, Clarke makes a point about its scope that the others miss: the words are not spoken of the widows only, but of the Church or its officers, and cannot be restricted to the widows, since the adjective is both of the masculine and of the feminine gender. Wesley defines the widow indeed as one who has no near relations to provide for her and who is wholly devoted to God, and gives the sharpest description of her opposite — delicately, voluptuously, in elegant, regular sensuality, though not in the use of any such pleasures as are unlawful in themselves.

Gill identifies the widow indeed by a Jewish distinction, as what the Jews call a perfect widow, in opposition to one that is divorced or to a brother's widow who has had the shoe plucked off for her. Of the contrasting figure he says only that she lives voluptuously and deliciously, a wanton, loose and licentious life, serving divers lusts and pleasures. On the charge with which the section closes, Gill lists what is being charged: the rebuking of persons of a different age and sex, the maintenance of widows, and particularly that children provide for their parents when helpless, and that widows trust in God and give themselves to prayer and supplication, and not live in sin.

8.pericope_label: If any provide not for his own, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel

schools.summary: Chrysostom takes the verse as a refutation of a whole way of thinking about salvation. Many consider that their own virtue is sufficient for their salvation, and that if they duly regulate their own life nothing further is wanting to save them; but in this they greatly err, which is proved by the example of him who buried his one talent, for he brought it back not diminished but entire, and just as it had been delivered to him. The provision the Apostle speaks of, Chrysostom insists, is universal, and relates to the soul as well as the body, since both are to be provided for; and he supports the duty from the prophet, who forbids a man to overlook his kinsmen of his own seed. He then presses the absurdity of neglecting them. If a man deserts those who are united by ties of kindred and affinity, how shall he be affectionate towards others? Will it not have the appearance of vainglory, when in benefiting others he slights his own relations and does not provide for them? And what will be said if, instructing others, he neglects his own, though he has greater facilities and a higher obligation to benefit them — will it not be said that these Christians are affectionate indeed, who neglect their own relatives? Chrysostom also explains why the comparison with the infidel bites: the unbeliever, if he benefits not aliens, at least does not neglect his near kindred.

Barnes reads the verse as a general rule drawn out of a particular duty, since the Apostle had been speaking particularly of the duty of children towards a widowed mother, and now gives the subject, as he often does, a general form: all ought to provide for those who are dependent on them, and if they did not, they had a less impressive sense of the obligations of duty than even the heathen had. He presses the force of the verb, which means to think beforehand: the man is to consider the probable wants of his own family and make arrangements to meet them, as God provides for our wants, seeing beforehand what we shall need and making the arrangements long in advance — the food we eat and the raiment we wear having been foreseen, and the plans of providence carried forward in the seasons, in the growth of animals, in the formation of fruit and in the bountiful harvest. The words 'his own', he adds, refer to those who are naturally dependent on a man, whether they live in his own immediate family or not, since there may be many distant relatives naturally dependent on our aid. Ellicott sees behind the warning a real situation in the Ephesian church, for in those early days, as now, men and women were attempting to persuade themselves that the hopes and promises of Christians could be attained by a mere profession of faith, by an assent to historical truths, by a barren reception of the doctrine of the atonement, without any practice of stern self-denial and apart from any loving consideration for others — there being evidently in that great Church not a few professed believers in the Crucified who, while possessed themselves of a competence and perhaps even of wealth, could calmly look on while their relations and friends languished in the deepest poverty. On the second clause he notes that the circle of those for whose support a Christian is responsible is enlarged, taking in relatives much more distant and even dependents connected with the family who had fallen into poverty and distress; and on the last he explains that faith, considered as a rule of life, is practically denied by one who neglects these kindly duties, since faith worketh by love. Robertson puts the same point grammatically: the perfect middle means that his act of impiety belies his claim to the faith, and the comparative sets him below one who makes no profession of piety at all.

Clarke explains why an unbeliever furnishes the standard of comparison: what are called the dictates of nature lead men to feel for and provide for their own families, and heathen writers are full of maxims of this kind — Tacitus saying that nature dictates that to every one his own children and relatives should be most dear, and Cicero that every man should take care of his own. He glosses the two clauses plainly, taking 'his own' as a man's own people or relatives, and 'those of his own house' as his own family, or a poor widow or relative who lives under his roof; and he takes the denial of the faith to mean the denial of the Christian religion, which strongly inculcates love and benevolence to all mankind. Wesley specifies what is to be provided, namely food and raiment, and for whom, namely the mother and grandmother who are desolate widows, and adds that such a man has denied the faith virtually — the faith which does not destroy but perfect natural duties. He then turns the verse against a use commonly made of it: what has this to do with heaping up money for our children, for which it is often so impertinently alleged? All men have their reasons for laying up money, he says: one will go to hell for fear of want, and another acts like a heathen lest he should be worse than an infidel.

Gill states the duty in its most concrete form, extending it in the direction the context requires: a man is to provide not only for his wife and children, but for his parents when they are grown old and cannot help themselves.

9.pericope_label: Let not a widow be taken into the number under threescore years old, well reported of for good works

schools.summary: Robertson renders the verb as to set down in an official list, an old word occurring only here in the New Testament, and translates the age clause as having become of no less than sixty years. This list of genuine widows, he says, apparently had some kind of church work attached to it — care for the sick, the orphans and the like — and on the marriage clause he is decided: widows on this list must not have been married a second time, though he grants that this interpretation is not so clear for the parallel requirements laid down earlier for bishops and deacons. He treats the good works of the following verse as a series of conditions of the first class, noting that each is a qualification for her work as a leader: the rearing of children, a late and rare word found only here; hospitality to strangers, another qualification for such leadership; the washing of the saints' feet, which he takes as proof of her hospitality and not as evidence of a church ordinance; and the relieving of the afflicted, an experience which qualified her for eleemosynary work. Barnes reconstructs the institution from the earliest notice of it, when at the first formation of the Christian church provision was made out of the public funds for the indigent widows belonging to it, and observes that Paul refers to the practice as to something well known and already existing. On the good works he takes the bringing up of children to mean either her own or others', the point being that it was done in a proper manner, and hospitality as a virtue greatly commended in the Scriptures. On the washing of feet he is careful: it is not certain whether this is to be understood literally or as merely denoting the performance of offices of a humble and self-denying kind, and since washing the feet of a guest was one of the rites of hospitality in the East, Paul may have spoken of it as literally performed — but there is not the slightest evidence that he refers to it as a religious rite or ordinance, any more than he does to the bringing up of children. Ellicott reconstructs the order itself, noting that here and here only in the New Testament is it alluded to, but that the instructions are so definite and so precise that it is impossible not to assume, in some if not all of the great churches, the existence of an official band of workers consisting of widows most carefully selected from the congregation, of somewhat advanced age, specially distinguished for devotion, and each possessing a high and stainless reputation — a distinct order, formally entered on the Church's list. On the good works he guards the first against a wooden reading: it must not be supposed that St. Paul deemed it necessary to exclude childless women from the order, only that the candidate must be well known as one who loves children and would gladly discharge any public duties to the little orphan ones of the flock entrusted to her care.

Gill dissents from the reading that makes this an order of deaconesses. Some choose to understand the words of the number of such as were made deaconesses, and had the care of the poor widows of the church committed to them, and the Arabic version renders it accordingly; but the former sense is best, since it appears that the Apostle is still speaking of widows to be relieved. Gill then gives practical reasons for the age limit: under sixty it might be supposed they would marry and so not be desolate but have husbands to provide for them, or they might be capable of labour and so of taking care of themselves — and he adds that the age of sixty years was by the Jews reckoned old age, but not under. On the good works he notes only that the widow was to be well reported of both by the members of the church and by them that are without.

Clarke sets out the three readings of the marriage clause and chooses between them: it may mean having lived in conjugal fidelity with her husband, or having had but one husband at a time, or, according to others, having never been married more than once. The first, he says, is the opinion of some of the most eminent of the Greek fathers, and appears to be that most consistent with the scope of the place and with truth. On the enrolment itself he leaves the question open between a list of those the Church must provide for and a list of deaconesses. On the good works he supplies the social background at two points. The phrase about bringing up children may well refer to the children of others, since it was customary among the Gentiles to expose their children when they were too poor to provide for them, and pious and humane people took these up and fed and clothed and educated them, so that the children so rescued were educated in the Christian faith by pious Christian women. And the washing of the saints' feet was an office of humanity shown to all strangers and travellers in the eastern countries, who, either walking barefoot or having only a sort of sole to defend the foot, needed washing when they came to their journey's end — pious women generally doing this act of kindness. Wesley takes the enrolment plainly as admission into the number of deaconesses, who attended sick women or travelling preachers, and adds a historical note, that afterwards they were admitted at forty if they were eminent for holiness; on the marriage clause he takes the widest of the three senses, that she had lived in lawful marriage, whether with one or more persons successively.

Henry states the principle behind the whole list of qualifications. Every one brought into any office in the church should be free from just censure; and many are proper objects of charity who yet ought not to be employed in public services. He reads the works themselves as reciprocal: those who would find mercy when they are in distress must show mercy when they are in prosperity, and those who show most readiness for every good work are most likely to be faithful in whatever is trusted to them. On the opposite disposition he is blunt — those who are idle very seldom are only idle, but make mischief among neighbours and sow discord among brethren. And he restates the reason for the whole arrangement: all believers are required to relieve those belonging to their families who are destitute, that the church may not be prevented from relieving such as are entirely destitute and friendless.

11.pericope_label: But the younger widows refuse; having damnation, because they have cast off their first faith

schools.summary: Barnes enters the strongest protest in the chapter against the received translation of the verb. There is probably a thought conveyed by the English words to most minds which is by no means in the original, and which does injustice both to the apostle and to the younger widows referred to: in the Greek there is no idea of wantonness in the sense of lasciviousness or lewdness, nor was that sense essential to the English word when the translation was made, since 'wanton' then meant wandering or roving in gaiety or sport, moving or flying loosely, playing in the wind. The Greek word, he notes, occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. On the refusal itself he is careful to limit it: it means only that Timothy was not to admit them into the class of widows under discussion, and cannot mean that he was to reject them as members of the church, or not to treat them with respect and kindness. On the word rendered damnation he objects likewise — it means rather condemnation, or the incurring of guilt, and does not of necessity mean that they would lose their souls; the meaning is that they would contract guilt if they had been admitted among this class of persons and then married again. The apostle does not say that marrying would be wrong in itself, or that they would be absolutely prohibited from it, but that injury would be done if they were admitted among the widows indeed, entrusted with the care of the younger women, and then left that situation: it might give occasion for scandal, it might break in upon the arrangements, and it would show a relaxing of the faith and of the deadness to the world which they were supposed to have. Robertson glosses the verb in the opposite direction from Barnes, taking it to mean to feel the impulse of sexual desire; it is a late compound, occurring only here and in Ignatius, and he records Souter's rendering, to exercise youthful vigour against Christ. On the following clause he takes 'their first faith' to mean their first pledge or contract to Christ, so that to reject it is like breaking the marriage contract — evidently one of the pledges on joining the order of widows was not to marry — and he notes the suggestion that the enrolment amounted to a kind of ordination such as deacons and bishops received. Ellicott insists that the exclusion is from office only, since the direction by no means shuts the younger women out from participation in the alms of the Church if they were in need and destitute, but wisely excluded them from a position and from duties which they might covet in their first days of grief and desolation, but of which, as experience had shown the Apostle, they not unfrequently wearied — those who put their hands to the plough and afterwards looked back being a hindrance to the Church's work and in some cases a subject of scandal and reproach. On the judgment threatened he agrees with Barnes that the Greek word is often unhappily translated, the context in each case deciding whether the judgment is favourable or the contrary; here it signifies that those who in after days give up a work which for their Master's sake they had undertaken expose themselves to a searching judgment, which will thoroughly sift the reasons that induced them to forsake the begun toil.

Clarke derives the disputed verb at length, from an intensive prefix and a verb meaning to act in a luxurious or wanton manner, and beyond that from words meaning to remove and the rein — a metaphor, he says, taken from a pampered horse from whose mouth the rein has been removed, so that there is nothing to check or confine him; and he judges the metaphor plain enough and the application easy. On the refusal he supplies the likely reason: those who were received into such a list probably promised to abide in their widowhood, and since young or comparatively young women might have both occasion and temptation to remarry, and so break their engagement to Christ, they should not be admitted — not that the apostle condemns their remarrying as a crime in itself, but because it was contrary to their engagement. On the judgment he agrees that the received word is wrong: in the sense in which we use it, he is satisfied the apostle never intended it, and it is likely that he refers to some promise or engagement made when they were taken on the list, so that the guilt is the guilt of having violated that promise. Casting off their first faith he explains in the same key, that by pledging their fidelity to a husband they have cast off their fidelity to Christ, a married life and their previous engagement being incompatible. Wesley reads the refusal simply as do not choose them, and takes the wantonness as directed against Christ, to whose more immediate service they had addicted themselves: they want to marry, and not with a single eye to the glory of God, and so withdraw themselves from that entire service of the church to which they were before engaged. On the rejected faith Wesley turns the phrase inward and makes it a question for every believer — they have deserted their trust in God and acted contrary to the first conviction, namely that wholly to devote themselves to his service was the most excellent way; for when we first receive power to believe, does not the Spirit of God generally point out what are the most excellent things, and at the same time give us a holy resolution to walk in the highest degree of Christian severity? And how unwise are we ever to sink into anything below it.

Chrysostom notices what the Apostle does not say, and thinks the silence deliberate. Having discoursed much concerning widows, having settled the age at which they were to be admitted and described their qualifications, Paul proceeds to refuse the younger; but concerning virgins, though the case of their falling is a much more gross one, he has said nothing of this kind — and rightly, Chrysostom says, for they had enrolled themselves on higher views, and the work with them proceeded from a greater elevation of mind. What is here required of widows as the receiving of strangers and the washing of the saints' feet he has represented, in the case of virgins, by attending upon the Lord without distraction, and by saying that the unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord.

Gill gives the two practical grounds for the refusal: the younger widows are fit for labour, and so can take care of themselves, and they may marry, as the apostle afterwards advises they should, and so would have husbands to take care of them. On the idleness that follows he supplies a Jewish description of the type, the woman the Jews call the gadding widow, who being at ease and without labour lives at the expense of the church and has nothing else to do but wander about from house to house.

13.pericope_label: They learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; I will therefore that the younger women marry

schools.summary: Clarke takes the catalogue of faults one word at a time and spares nothing. They learn to be idle: they do not love work, and they will not work. Wandering about from house to house is gadding and gossiping, never contented with home, always visiting. And if it went no farther this would be intolerable, but they are tattlers — tale-bearers, whisperers, light trifling persons, all noise and no work; busybodies, persons who meddle with the concerns of others and mind every one's business but their own; speakers of things they ought not, meaning lies, slanders and calumnies, backbiting their neighbours and everywhere sowing the seed of dissension. On the remedy he refuses to let the point be blurred: since the preceding discourse has been about the younger widows, it is most evident that by the younger women the apostle means them, and here the apostle, so far from forbidding second marriages, positively enjoins or at least recommends them — and what man of sense, Clarke asks, could have done otherwise in the cases he mentions? It is no sin in any case to marry, bear children and take care of a family, but it is a sin in every case to be idle. He considers these women unfit for the office of the female diaconate, and therefore wills them to marry, educate children, and give themselves wholly up to domestic affairs. On the backsliding of the fifteenth verse he adds a sentence worth keeping: slight deviations, in the first instance, from a right line may lead at last to an infinite distance from Christ. And on the last verse he states the purpose of the whole arrangement — let Christians relieve their own poor widows and not burden the Church with their maintenance, that the funds may be spared for the support of those widows who were employed in its service, teaching children and visiting the sick. Wesley reads the counsel to marry as addressed to widows or virgins, such as are not disposed to live single, and gives the practical effect: then will they have sufficient employment of their own, and give no occasion of reproach to the adversary, whether Jew or heathen.

Barnes cautions against reading the charge of idleness as a judgment on widows as a class: the apostle does not mean that widows are naturally disposed to be idle, but that in the situation referred to there would be danger of it, since there would be a security in the age and established habits of those more advanced in life which there could not be in the case of the younger. On the counsel to marry he is equally careful: Paul gives it as his opinion or counsel, and we are not to suppose that he gives it as an absolute and universal command, for it might not always be at the option of a widow to marry again, and it cannot be doubted that there may be cases where it would be unadvisable — but he speaks of it as a general rule, it being better for such persons to have domestic concerns requiring their attention. On the fifteenth verse he explains that some had already followed the great Tempter rather than the Lord Jesus, and that this is stated as a reason why they should not be admitted into the number of the widows maintained at the expense of the church. On the last verse he draws the plain moral: nothing can be more unreasonable than to leave those who are properly dependent on us to be supported by others when we are able to maintain them ourselves. Ellicott traces how the danger would arise from the work itself: the first fervour of their devotion and renunciation of self will have cooled, and their very occupation will become a snare to them, since the going about to the various dwellings for the object of consoling, instructing and assisting would give them, now that their minds were no longer exclusively turned to religious thoughts, many an opportunity of wasting precious hours and of indulging in frivolous, if not in harmful, conversation. On the counsel to marry he reads a deliberate warning against premature asceticism: the Apostle expresses his will that in these Christian communities the younger widows should not, in the first fervour of their zeal and while borne down by sorrow, attempt anything like an ascetic life which they would probably tire of after a season, and so in the long run injure rather than benefit the cause of Christ — St. Paul's practical mind, guided by the Spirit of God, having left us no impossible rules of perfection, no exaggerated praises of asceticism, and no passionate exhortings to a life made up entirely of self-sacrifice. On the backsliding he thinks the failure recent and the silence merciful, since the Apostle, though these unhappy sisters had worked such great mischief to the cause of Christ, forbore to mention any by name. Robertson notes the Greek idiom by which there is no verb 'to be' in the phrase about idleness, an unusual construction paralleled in Plato and Dio Chrysostom, and calls the picture of wandering around the houses a vivid one of idle tattlers and gossipers; on the counsel to marry he observes what the third verb concedes, since the wife is here put as ruler of the household, a proper recognition of her influence and what Liddon called a new and improved position.

Gill takes the counsel to marry as addressed to the younger widows in particular rather than to young women in general, though he allows that it will suit them too. On the turning aside after Satan he widens the phrase into a rule: the apostle means those younger widows whom he knew and had observed to have departed from the faith they first professed, and to have turned their backs on Christ; and everyone who apostatizes from a profession of Christ and follows either false teachers and their doctrines, such as the Gnostics who condemned marriage, or any sinful and impure way of life, may be said to turn aside after Satan. On the last verse he identifies who is addressed — any member of a church, whether a brother or a sister, who has mothers or grandmothers or any near relations widows, in mean circumstances and incapable of taking care of themselves.

17.pericope_label: Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word

schools.summary: Gill establishes who is meant by elimination, since the word has just been used in another sense. These are not elders in age — though such ought to be honoured and respected, and to have a proper maintenance either from their children or from the church when they are reduced and incapable of helping themselves, that being what should be done for all such persons, whereas the elders here are particularly described as good rulers and labourers in the word and doctrine, and elders in age have been taken notice of before. Nor are civil magistrates intended, such as were called the elders of Israel, for though such as discharge that office well are worthy of honour, it does not belong to any of them to labour in preaching the doctrine of the Gospel. Nor are deacons designed, for they are never called elders in Scripture, their work is not ruling but serving of tables, the ministry of the word does not belong to them as such, and no maintenance is allowed them from the church on account of their office. Nor, finally, are lay elders meant, who rule but teach not, since Gill holds there are no such officers appointed in the churches of Christ, whose only officers are bishops or elders and deacons.

Clarke takes the word here as the name of an ecclesiastical officer, similar to what we now term presbyter, and supports the identification from Macknight, who observed that in the first age the name elder was given to all who exercised any sacred office in the Church — the same persons being called bishops in one verse of Acts who were called elders in another, the same in Titus, and all who held sacred offices in Lystra being called collectively the presbytery or eldership. On the honour he is unambiguous: almost every critic of note allows that the word here signifies reward, stipend or wages, so that the sense is, let him have a double or a larger salary who rules well. And he gives the reason, which is not merely that the man deserves it: in the discharge of his office he must be at expense in proportion to his diligence, in visiting and relieving the sick, in lodging and providing for strangers — in a word, in that hospitality which was required of every bishop or presbyter. Especially, he adds, is this due to those who not only preach publicly but instruct privately. Wesley describes the elders that rule well as those who approve themselves faithful stewards of all that is committed to their charge, and reads the double honour as a more abundant provision, seeing that such men will employ it all to the glory of God. He then adds a piece of church history which cuts against the practice that grew out of the text: since it was the most laborious and disinterested men who were put into these offices, whatever any one had to bestow, in his life or at his death, was generally lodged in their hands for the poor — by which means the churchmen became very rich in after ages, but as the design of the donors was something else, there is the highest reason why it should be disposed of according to their pious intent. Those who labour, he glosses, means those who labour diligently and painfully, in teaching the word.

Barnes places the verse in the letter's structure, the Apostle having given full instructions respecting bishops, deacons and widows, and proceeding here to describe the duty of the church towards those who sustain the office of elder. The word properly refers to age, and is then used to denote the officers of the church, probably because the aged were at first entrusted with the administration of its affairs; and it was in familiar use among the Jews to denote the body of men that presided in the synagogue. To rule well is to preside well, or to manage well the spiritual interests of the church, the verb meaning to be over or to preside over or to have the care of, and being used elsewhere of bishops and of an apostle — a word that would apply to any officers to whom the management and government of the church was entrusted. Barnes adds the historical caution that it is probable not precisely the same organisation was pursued in every place where a church was established. Robertson identifies the elder here with the bishop, in the same sense as in the third chapter and in Titus, citing Luke's use of the word where Paul says bishops, and takes the participle as a second perfect active used intransitively. On the honour he canvasses the proposals rather than deciding: White suggests remuneration rather than honour, since the word is commonly used for price or pay; Liddon proposes honorarium, as covering both honour and pay and so answering to the word 'double'; Wetstein gives numerous examples of soldiers receiving double pay for unusual services; and some suggest simply twice the pay given the enrolled widows. On the last clause he takes those who labour in word and teaching to be either those who work hard at preaching and teaching, or those who teach and preach and do not merely preside. Ellicott is chiefly interested in what the passage shows about Timothy's own position: to use the title of Bishop in the ecclesiastical sense would be as yet an anachronism, though it probably was of general use within thirty years of the letter, but one in Timothy's position evidently had the distribution of the several grades of honours and remuneration among the presbyteral order, and to him as presiding elder belonged the functions of supreme judge in all matters ecclesiastical and moral relating to the officials of both sexes connected with the Church.

Henry reads the verse as a direction concerning the supporting of ministers, care being taken that they be honourably maintained: to be counted worthy of double honour is to be counted worthy of double maintenance, double to what they have had or to what others have, and especially those who are more laborious than others. He then makes an observation which decides the disputed question against his own tradition. The presbytery ruled, and the same men that ruled were those who laboured in the word and doctrine: they had not one to preach to them and another to rule them, but the work was done by one and the same person. Some have imagined that by the elders that rule well the apostle means lay-elders, employed in ruling but not in teaching, concerned in church government but not meddling with the administration of the word and sacraments — and Henry confesses that this is the plainest text of scripture that can be found to countenance such an opinion. Yet he will not take it: it seems a little strange that mere ruling elders should be accounted worthy of double honour, when the apostle preferred preaching to baptizing and would much more prefer it to ruling the church, and it is stranger still that the apostle should take no notice of such officers where he treats of church officers directly.

18.pericope_label: The labourer is worthy of his reward; against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses

schools.summary: Barnes reads the first quotation as the ground of the church's duty: as God took care to make provision for the labouring ox, much more should due attention be paid to those who labour for the welfare of the church. On the second he raises a question of canon. The saying is found substantially in Matthew and in Luke; it does not occur in so many words in the Old Testament; and yet the apostle adduces it evidently as a quotation from the Scriptures and as authority in the case — from which it would seem probable that he had seen the gospel by Matthew or by Luke, and that he quoted this as a part of Scripture and regarded the book as such. On the rule about accusations Barnes observes that Paul supposed Timothy would be called on to hear charges against others in the ministerial office and to express his judgment on them, but that there is no reason to suppose he meant that Timothy should hear them alone, or as a prelate, the counsel being just such as would now be given to a Presbyterian or Congregational minister, or to an associate justice. On the public rebuke he marks the limits of the power precisely: it means a public statement of the nature of the offence, and such censure as the case demands, but it extends only to spiritual censures, and there is no power given of inflicting any punishment by fine or imprisonment — the power of the church in such cases being only to express its strong and decided disapprobation of the wrong done, and, if the case demands it, to disown the offending member or minister. Robertson supplies the philology, noting that the first quotation is from Deuteronomy and is cited elsewhere by Paul for the same purpose, to show the preacher's right to pay for his work, and that the second occurs in precisely this form in Luke and in a slightly different form in Matthew. Whether Paul is here quoting an unwritten saying of Jesus, as he does in Acts, or the Gospel of Luke, or the collection of the sayings, there is, he says, no way to decide the question. On the accusation he notes the double construction of the exception and the idiomatic use of the preposition, upon the basis of; and on the public rebuke he adds the qualification that keeps it from becoming something else — public rebuke when there is a clear case, not promiscuous gossip. Ellicott takes the elder here for the presbyter, the ordained minister of the Church, and names the likely occasions of such charges, which owe much to jealousy, party feeling and suspected doctrinal error; every possible precaution is to be taken against merely vexatious charges brought against one occupying so hard a position. He reads the following verse as still referring exclusively to that order of presbyters, and states the principle behind the severity: the errors and sins of teachers of the faith are far more dangerous than those of the men who make up the rank and file of congregations, so that when they are proved to be continuing in sin their punishment must be as marked as in the other case was the reward.

Clarke takes the first quotation as a manifest proof that by honour in the preceding verse the apostle means salary or wages, and then turns the argument in both directions with some vigour. The maintenance of every man in the Church should be in proportion to his own labour and the necessities of his family; he that does no work should have no wages; and in the Church of Christ there never can be a sinecure. They who minister at the altar should live by the altar, the ox that treadeth out the corn should not be muzzled, and the labourer is worthy of his hire — but the altar should not support him who does not minister at it, and if the ox will not tread out the corn, let him go to the common or be muzzled; if the man will not labour, let him have no hire. On the rule about accusations he explains the reason for the special protection: be very cautious of receiving evil reports against those whose business it is to preach to others and correct their vices, and do not consider an elder guilty of any alleged crime unless it be proved by two or three witnesses. He finds a Roman parallel worth noting, that among the Romans a plebeian might be condemned on the deposition of one credible witness but it required two to convict a senator, the reason for the difference being evident, since those whose business it is to correct others will usually have many enemies. On the public rebuke he takes the rebuke to be before the members of the Church, which was the custom of the Jews in their synagogues, though if the words refer to the elders alone then the transgressing elder is to be reproved before his fellows and tried by them; and he states the object of all church censures — to reclaim the transgressors, and to give warning to others. Wesley finds a Mosaic parallel to the same rule: by the Mosaic law a private person might be cited, though not condemned, on the testimony of one witness, but St. Paul forbids an elder to be even cited on such evidence, his reputation being of more importance than that of others. On the rebuke he specifies both the offenders and the audience — those elders that sin scandalously, and are duly convicted, are to be rebuked before the church.

Gill is emphatic that the protection given to elders is not a shelter. He takes the accusation to be a charge of any crime, and then insists that the Apostle was far from screening wicked ministers or elders guilty of flagitious crimes and gross enormities: though the words about rebuking may be applied to all offenders who are members of churches, they seem chiefly to regard elders — even such as sin, who continue to sin, who live in sin, in some notorious sin which is evident and known, to the great scandal of religion and the dishonour of the Gospel. He records an alternative construction of the clause, that some read it as 'them that sin before all, rebuke'; and he takes the rebuke to mean not merely admonishing once and again, but degrading such men from their office, withdrawing from them as from other disorderly persons, and cutting them off and casting them out of the church in a public manner — which the Arabic version renders as before the congregation.

21.pericope_label: I charge thee before God and the elect angels; lay hands suddenly on no man, keep thyself pure

schools.summary: Chrysostom explains why the solemnity is introduced at this point. Having spoken of bishops and deacons, of men and of women, of widows and elders and of all others, and having shown how great was the authority of a bishop, the Apostle now comes to speak of judgment, and so adds the charge — and he charges him fearfully. For though Timothy was his beloved son, Paul did not therefore stand in awe of him: as he was not ashamed to say of himself that he feared lest, having preached to others, he should himself be a castaway, much less would he be afraid or ashamed in the case of Timothy. He calls the Father and the Son to witness what he has said, making his appeal to them against that future Day. As for the elect angels, Chrysostom explains their addition from great moderation, comparing Moses who said, I call heaven and earth to witness, and the prophet who said, Hear ye, O mountains, and strong foundations of the earth.

Barnes explains the force of the verb, which means properly to call to witness, then to affirm with solemn attestations, and then to admonish solemnly and to urge earnestly — a word implying that the subject is of great importance. Paul gives this charge as in the presence of God, of the Redeemer and of the elect angels, and wishes to secure that sense of solemnity which must arise from the presence of such holy witnesses; and Barnes presses the thought on his own readers, since it is not uncommon in the Scriptures to speak as if we were in the presence of holy angels and of the disembodied spirits of the good, no one can prove that they are not witnesses of what we do, and it is at all events right to urge on others the performance of duty as if the eye of a departed father or mother or sister were fixed upon us. On the laying on of hands he sets aside two readings — that it means laying hands on the sick, or absolving penitents — in favour of the obvious meaning, ordination, since it was usual to lay hands on the heads of those ordained to a sacred office. The idea, he says, is that Timothy should not be hasty in an act so important as introducing men to the ministry, but should take time to give them a fair trial of their piety and should have satisfactory evidence of their qualifications, not introducing a man merely because he gave evidence of piety, or burned with ardent zeal, or thought himself qualified; and Barnes notes that while this shows Timothy had the right to ordain, it does not show that he ordained alone or as a prelate. Ellicott renders the charge more forcibly as 'I solemnly charge thee', notes that the word Lord should be omitted before Jesus Christ on the older authorities, and reads the whole as an adjuration to carry out the government of the Church of Ephesus impartially, doing nothing hastily and ever watchful of himself. Having just pressed on Timothy the care needed in the case of an accused presbyter, Paul now reminds him of the ever-present unseen witnesses of his conduct: in that awful presence, in sight of the throne of God with Messiah on the right hand and the angels gathering round about the throne, would Timothy guide and rule the congregations of Christians in that famous Eastern city. On the laying on of hands Ellicott takes the wider view, that while the command refers primarily to the solemn laying on of hands at the ordination of presbyters and deacons, it no doubt also includes the laying on of hands customary, apparently even in the Apostolic age, on the absolution of penitents and their re-admission to church fellowship — for to limit the reference to ordination alone would imply a greater corruption in the church at that early date than is credible. By negligently admitting unfit persons into the ministry, or by carelessly readmitting to fellowship those who by their evil life had forfeited it, Timothy would incur a grave responsibility and would in fact be a partaker in the sins of those men. Robertson takes 'elect' in the sense of the holy angels who kept their own principality and did not sin, and notes Paul's interest in angels elsewhere; he glosses the two conditions as late and rare words meaning without prejudgment and by inclining towards one; and on the laying on of hands he declines to choose, observing that it is not clear whether the case is that of ministers just ordained, or a warning against the hasty ordination of untried men, or the recognition and restoration of deposed ministers — the prohibition suiting either situation, or both.

Clarke would have Timothy consider that all he did should be done as in the sight of God, the Father of the spirits of all flesh, in the sight of Christ, the Saviour of sinners who purchased the Church with his own blood, and in the sight of the most holy and eminent angels, whose office it was to minister to the heirs of salvation. On the word elect applied to the angels he reports the received view, that it distinguishes those who stood when others fell from their first estate, the former being elect or approved and the latter reprobate or disapproved, though he adds that perhaps there is nothing else meant than the angels chosen out from among others by the Lord himself to be ministering servants to the Church. The two conditions he renders entirely practically: without prejudice means promote no man's cause, and make not up thy mind on any case till thou hast weighed both sides and heard both parties with their respective witnesses, and then act impartially as the matter may appear to be proved. On the laying on of hands he is equally plain — do not hastily appoint any person to the sacred ministry, but let the person be well proved before he receives the imposition of hands — and he draws out the responsibility of those who ordain, since it is a sin for any improper person to thrust himself into the sacred office, and he partakes of that sin who introduces him, helps him forward, or sanctions him in it. Clarke closes with an exclamation over the account that rash, undiscerning and prejudiced bishops and presbyters will have to render to God for their ordinations, laying careless hands on those who cannot teach and will not learn, while probably refusing to induct others well qualified for the Christian ministry. Wesley refers the charge to the last judgment, in which we shall stand before God and Christ with his elect, that is, holy angels, who are the witnesses of our conversation — and observes that the Apostle here looks through his own labours, and even through time itself, and seems to stand as one already in eternity. The two conditions he glosses as passing no sentence till the cause is fully heard, and none for or against any one; and the laying on of hands as appointing no man to church offices without full trial and examination, since otherwise Timothy would be accessary to, and accountable for, his misbehaviour in office.

Gill grounds the solemnity of the charge in the character of the one before whom it is made: God sees and knows all things, and is a righteous and most impartial Judge, with whom there is no respect of persons, and in whose place and stead the judges of the earth, both civil and ecclesiastical, stand, and to whom they are accountable for the judgment they pass on men and things. It was in God's house or church that Timothy was, doing his business, which ought to be done with a view to his glory — and the apostle therefore gives him this solemn charge as in his sight. On the laying on of hands Gill argues for ordination alone against the alternative: it is not to be understood of removing censures from offenders upon their repentance, which it seems in later times has been done by imposition of hands, since no such custom obtained in the apostle's time and a taking off of censures is never in Scripture signified by this phrase; rather it means the admission of persons into the work of the ministry and their installation in the office of a pastor, upon whom in these early times hands were laid by the apostles, whereby gifts were conveyed, as they were on Timothy himself.

23.pericope_label: Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach’s sake and thine often infirmities

schools.summary: Barnes takes up the difficulty everyone feels about the verse's position, noting that many have considered it so great that they suppose the verse displaced and belonging in some other connection. The true reason for its introduction here, he thinks, is that Paul was suddenly impressed with the thought — a thought very likely to come over a man who is writing on the duties of the ministry — of the arduous nature of the ministerial office. He was giving counsels about an office which required a great amount of labour, care and anxiety; the labours enjoined were such as to demand all a man's time, and the care and anxiety incident to such a charge would be very likely to prostrate the frame and injure the health. Then he remembered that Timothy was yet but a youth, recalled his feebleness of constitution and his frequent attacks of illness, and recollected the very abstemious habits which he had prescribed for himself — and in that connection urges on him a careful regard for his health, prescribing the use of a small quantity of wine as a suitable medicine in his case. Robertson renders the first clause as be no longer a water-drinker, a verb occurring only here in the New Testament, and states the limit exactly: this is not a call away from complete asceticism, but only the urging of some wine in Timothy's peculiar physical condition, a sort of medical prescription for this case, with the emphasis falling on the words 'a little'. He glosses the noun for stomach, which is old and means in Homer the throat or opening of the stomach and in Plutarch the stomach itself, and the adjective rendered often, which is an old word meaning dense or frequent; and he concludes that Timothy was clearly a semi-invalid. Ellicott turns the oddity of the verse into an argument for the letter's authenticity. Those who argue that this Epistle was the artificial composition of an age subsequent to St. Paul's, written in great measure to support a hierarchical development of the following century, have no little difficulty in accounting for the presence of such a command; it can in fact only be explained on the supposition that the letter was in truth written by St. Paul to Timothy in all freedom and in all love — by the older and more experienced to the younger and comparatively untried man, by the master to the pupil, by an old and trusted friend accustomed to speak his whole mind. No ecclesiastical forger of the second or third century, he says, would have dreamed, or, had he dreamed, would have dared, to weave into the complicated tapestry of such an Epistle a charge like this one. He adds that the reminder was no doubt suggested by St. Paul's own words just before, when he closed his direction about the laying on of hands by telling Timothy to keep himself pure.

Clarke reports that the whole verse seems to several learned critics and divines strangely inserted in this place, and might have been, according to them, a note which the apostle inserted in the margin of his letter on recollecting the precarious state of Timothy's health and his great abstemiousness and self-denial; but he states his own judgment against them, believing the verse to be in its proper place and, for the reasons he gives, not less necessary than the directions which precede and follow it. He then inquires into the reasons for the advice itself, and finds them in the widespread religious avoidance of wine. The priests under the Mosaic law were forbidden, while performing sacred rites, to drink wine or strong drink when they went into the tabernacle of the congregation, lest they die, and this was made a statute for ever throughout their generations; it was the same with the Egyptian priests; and it was forbidden also among the Romans, and particularly to women and young persons, Clarke citing Plato's proposal in the Laws that boys should not taste wine at all before eighteen, and only in moderation until thirty.

Cyril of Jerusalem takes the verse into a wider set of ordinances about food, and uses it to restrain both parties in a dispute about eating. Concerning food, he says, let these be your ordinances, since in regard to meats also many stumble: for some deal indifferently with things offered to idols, while others discipline themselves but condemn those that eat, and in different ways men's souls are defiled in the matter of meats, from ignorance of the useful reasons for eating and for not eating. He then states what fasting is for, and it is not contempt of the creature: we fast by abstaining from wine and flesh, not because we abhor them as abominations, but because we look for our reward — that having scorned things sensible we may enjoy a spiritual and intellectual feast, and that having now sown in tears we may reap in joy in the world to come. From this he draws the double prohibition which makes this verse his own: despise not therefore them that eat, and who because of the weakness of their bodies partake of food, nor yet blame those who use a little wine for their stomach's sake and their often infirmities; and neither condemn the men as sinners, nor abhor the flesh as strange food. He appeals in support to the Apostle, who knows some of this sort when he speaks of those forbidding to marry and commanding to abstain from meats which God created to be received with thanksgiving by them that believe.

Gill balances the two duties the verse holds together. It was commendable in Timothy to keep under his body, as the apostle did, by abstemious living, and not to pamper the flesh and encourage the lusts of it, and so to preserve purity and chastity; yet it was proper that he should take care of his health, that it should not be impaired by too much severity, and so leave him incapable of doing the work of the Lord. And it seems by this direction, Gill observes, that Timothy's long and only use of water for his drink had been prejudicial to his health, which is why the following advice was judged proper.

24.pericope_label: Some men’s sins are open beforehand, going before to judgment; and the good works of some are manifest beforehand

schools.summary: Clarke reads the two verses as a practical sorting of the candidates Timothy would actually meet. Among them he would find, first, some of whom he knew nothing but that they professed Christianity, and these were to be tried before being appointed; second, some of whose faith and piety he had the fullest knowledge, and whose usefulness in the Church was well known; and third, some whose lives were not at all, or but partially, reformed, who were still unchanged in their hearts and unholy in their lives. The sins of these last were known to all, and it is they that go before to judgment, so that with them Timothy could have no difficulty. With the first class he must have more difficulty, since there might have been hypocrites among them whose sins could not be known until after they had been brought into the sacred office; the sins of others might be found out after, or in consequence of, investigation; and those that were otherwise could not be long hid from his knowledge or from the knowledge of the Church. On all these accounts, Clarke concludes, the exhortation was necessary: lay hands suddenly on no man. On the good works he writes with evident affection for the obscure: though those who are very holy and very useful in the Church cannot be unknown, there are others not less holy who need to be brought forward, who do much good in private, and whose character and good works are not fully known till after diligent inquiry — these being they who do not let their left hand know what their right hand does. Clarke closes the chapter by admitting how much of it remains unsettled, saying that after so long and minute an examination of its subjects little remains to be added, and that the whole account concerning the widows — who they were, what their provision, what their occupation, and how they were supported — are to him questions of considerable difficulty, on which he has given the best account in his power. On the imposition of hands, or what he calls vulgarly but improperly ordination, he states a conviction that separates him from the other witnesses: what is said on this subject in the chapter, and indeed in the epistle, is rather to be understood prophetically, and was intended for a much later age of the Christian Church. Wesley reads the first clause as meaning that some men's sins are manifest before any strict inquiry be made, going before to judgment so that Timothy may immediately judge them unworthy of any spiritual office, while the sins of others follow after, more covertly; and he draws the same rule from the hidden good works, which cannot be long hid from Timothy's knowledge — on which account also, he says, be not hasty in laying on of hands.

Barnes reads the declaration, though general in form, in connection with the subject of introducing men to the ministry, treating the verse about wine as parenthetical. The character of some men is manifest, there being no disguise and no danger of mistake about it, since their conduct is apparent to all; and about such men Timothy ought not to hesitate a moment, but, no matter what their talents or learning or rank in the community, ought to have no participation in introducing them to the ministry. Their character is so well understood that there is no need of waiting for the day of judgment to know what they are, their deeds so preceding their own appearance at the judgment-bar that the record and the verdict can be made up before they arrive there. On the other side the character of some is equally clear, and there can be no doubt from their works that they are good men: we need not wait for the day of judgment to determine that, but may treat them here as good men and introduce them to offices which only good men can fill. And those who are otherwise cannot be ultimately concealed or misunderstood, for there are arrangements in the divine government for bringing out the character of every man — some good men spreading such a glory around them that no one can mistake what they are, while others are modest, retiring, unobtrusive and unknown, living in obscurity and with slender means. Robertson glosses the first adjective as openly plain, plain before all, an old word occurring only here and in Hebrews, and takes the sins to be so plain that they receive instant condemnation; the others, he says, dog a man's steps, not clearly manifest at first but coming out plainly at last — how true, he adds, that is of secret sins. On the good works that have it otherwise, meaning deeds not clearly manifest, he finds comfort for modest preachers and other believers whose good deeds are not known and not blazoned forth: they will come out in the end. Ellicott reads the passage as the close of the whole subject on which the Apostle had been instructing his representative at Ephesus, telling him that in his choice of men to fill public positions, in his public inquiries into their conduct and teaching, and in his inquiries respecting sinners seeking readmission to church fellowship, he must not forget that there are two classes of sins — the one public and open, heralds of the judgment to follow, in whose case the chief pastor would have no difficulty in determining his course of action, and the other silent and, so far as public knowledge goes, unknown, published only after judgment has been given, the right estimating of which will require much care and penetration. On the good works he hears an encouragement addressed to Timothy's own fears, since in his difficult post he might dread lest true nobility of character should escape his notice and the best and truest never be enrolled on the register of church officers: St. Paul bids him take courage in the thought that in many a case self-sacrifice, generosity and stern principle will be sufficiently manifest to guide him in choosing fit persons for the holy calling, and that in those rarer cases where the higher and sweeter virtues are hidden, he may be sure that in God's good season these too will become known to him, in ample time for him to call them also into his Master's service. Ellicott also records a suggestion, made with considerable ingenuity, that the last verse belongs to and introduces a new division of the Epistle rather than closing this one.

Gill puts the practical upshot of both verses in the same form. Some men are such open and notorious sinners that there is no need of any inquiry about them, or any examination of them, or any witnesses to be called to their character in order to pass judgment concerning them; they even prevent and supersede any formal process about them — so that should they be proposed for the ministry, Timothy would know at once what to do with them, namely reject them, and there would be no danger of his laying hands suddenly on such. On the other side, the characters of some men are so fair and bright, and it is so clear a point that they have received the grace of God in truth, that they have rich furniture for the ministry, that they are sound in the doctrine of faith and are men of godly life and conversation, that they likewise prevent any formal inquiry, examination and judgment, and there can be no difficulty in admitting them at once. The rule about laying on hands, Gill concludes, is therefore not designed for either of these plain cases, but to guard against those with whom things do not appear so very clear and manifest.
